facts.fact: The lowest unit rate is a pricing protection established by the FCC under Section 315(b) of the Communications Act (47 U.S.C. SS 315).
facts.quote: The lowest unit rate (LUR) is a pricing protection established by the Federal Communications Commission under Section 315(b) of the Communications Act (47 U.S.C. SS 315).

facts.fact: Under the lowest unit rate, broadcast TV and radio stations may charge legally qualified candidates no more than the lowest rate charged to any other advertiser for the same class and amount of time in the same time period.
facts.quote: It requires broadcast television and radio stations to charge legally qualified candidates no more than the lowest rate the station charges any other advertiser for the same class and amount of time

facts.fact: The lowest unit rate applies during a window of 45 days before a primary election, including runoffs and special primaries.
facts.quote: 45 days before a primary election (including runoffs and special primaries)

facts.fact: The lowest unit rate applies during a window of 60 days before a general election.
facts.quote: 60 days before a general election

facts.fact: Outside the lowest unit rate windows, candidates are only entitled to 'comparable' rates, which the page describes as a weaker protection.
facts.quote: Outside these windows, candidates are only entitled to "comparable" rates

facts.fact: The page states that in a general election, the 60-day LUR window typically begins in early September and runs through Election Day in November.
facts.quote: the 60-day LUR window typically begins in early September and runs through Election Day in November

facts.fact: The page claims that during a heated cycle, market rates bought in July for a November election can be two to three times higher than LUR pricing.
facts.quote: during a heated cycle can be two to three times higher than LUR pricing

facts.fact: Political Action Committees (super PACs, traditional PACs, and hybrid PACs) pay market rates regardless of when they buy and do not qualify for LUR.
facts.quote: Super PACs, traditional PACs, and hybrid PACs pay market rates regardless of when they buy.

facts.fact: Under the page's example, a car dealership paying $200 for a 30-second spot during the 6 p.m. news sets the lowest rate for that class and amount of time, which an eligible candidate would receive during the election window.
facts.quote: If a car dealership pays $200 for a 30-second spot during the 6 p.m. news, and that is the lowest rate for the same class and amount of time

facts.fact: For preemptible-with-notice time, stations can bump a spot with advance notice, often 2 weeks.
facts.quote: Station can bump your spot with advance notice (often 2 weeks)

facts.fact: The lowest unit rate is calculated independently for each broadcast time class, so the LUR for non-preemptible time is higher than for immediately preemptible time.
facts.quote: So the LUR for non-preemptible time will be higher than the LUR for immediately preemptible time.

facts.fact: Under FCC rules, stations must keep their political files publicly accessible, and these files include rate information and invoices.
facts.quote: Under FCC rules, stations must keep their political files publicly accessible.

facts.fact: The lowest unit rate applies only to broadcast television and radio stations licensed by the FCC and does not apply to cable networks, streaming platforms, or CTV.
facts.quote: the lowest unit rate applies only to broadcast television and radio stations licensed by the FCC. It does not apply to cable networks, streaming platforms, or Connected TV (CTV).

facts.fact: The page defines early morning daypart as 6-9 a.m., early fringe/news as 4-8 p.m., and primetime as 8-11 p.m.
facts.quote: Early morning (6-9 a.m.): Local news audiences, strong for reaching older voters

facts.fact: The page's guide was published on March 1, 2026.
Market-based CTV pricing is typically $15-35 CPM according to the page.
facts.quote: Market-based pricing (typically $15-35 CPM), but with precision targeting.

facts.fact: Adwave states that its platform has a minimum spend of $30 a day.
facts.quote: With a minimum spend of just $30 a day and access to 100+ premium streaming networks

facts.fact: The page states that the lowest unit rate window begins 45 days before a primary election.
facts.quote: The LUR window begins 45 days before a primary election and 60 days before a general election.

facts.fact: The page states that for the 2026 general election in November, the 60-day LUR window would start in early September.
facts.quote: For the 2026 general election in November, the 60-day window would start in early September.

facts.fact: Under the page's example, a district covering 15% of a major TV market would waste 85% of a broadcast buy on viewers who cannot vote for the candidate.
facts.quote: a district that covers just 15% of a major TV market would waste 85% of their broadcast buy on viewers who can't vote for them.

facts.fact: The page suggests a typical candidate campaign allocation during the LUR window of 60-70% broadcast and 30-40% CTV.
facts.quote: A typical allocation for a candidate campaign during the LUR window might look like 60-70% broadcast (taking advantage of LUR rates) and 30-40% CTV

facts.fact: Under FCC Section 315(b), legally qualified candidates are entitled to the lowest unit rate during defined pre-election windows, according to the page.
facts.quote: Under FCC Section 315(b), legally qualified candidates are entitled to this rate during defined pre-election windows.

facts.fact: The page states that the lowest unit rate does not apply to streaming TV or CTV ads, which are market-priced.
facts.quote: No. The lowest unit rate is an FCC regulation that applies only to broadcast television and radio stations

facts.fact: The page states that broadcast stations must maintain public political files with the FCC, accessible at publicfiles.fcc.gov.
facts.quote: Broadcast stations are required to maintain public political files with the FCC, accessible at publicfiles.fcc.gov.
